overview: This file combines a January 1941 cross-reference concerning false news reports and the withdrawal of an American citizen with an April 1940 State Department memorandum summarizing a Tokyo Embassy report on Japanese press censorship. The memorandum describes the suppression of a magazine article by a Japanese Foreign Office official who challenged official conceptions of the “China Incident,” Japanese hegemony over China, pan-Asianism, and the “new order in East Asia.” The Division of Far Eastern Affairs regarded the episode as evidence of conflict within the Japanese government and of growing recognition that Japan lacked the resources to dominate China and alienate Europe and the United States.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on false reports and withdrawal of an American citizen
subfiles.from: U.S. Department of State filing office
subfiles.about: A filing sheet directs researchers to an original communication addressed to Japan concerning false reports and the withdrawal of an American citizen or news correspondent.
subfiles.summary: The sheet cross-references original paper no. 2110, dated January 28, 1941, and addressed to Japan through Grew. Its subject notation refers to the withdrawal of an American citizen and news despatches, while its précis states that the communication refuted false reports and requested that they be brought to the attention of the Japanese authorities. The original was filed as 390.1115a/317.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on a suppressed Japanese critique of China policy
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs, U.S. Department of State
subfiles.to: Not stated; routed through the Law Division and to Mr. Weller
subfiles.about: The memorandum summarizes Tokyo telegram no. 4595 concerning the suppression of a Foreign Office official's article criticizing Japan's objectives and strategy in China.
subfiles.summary: A Japanese-language magazine was suppressed after publishing an article by a Foreign Office official, who was subsequently forced to resign. The author argued that the fighting in China was a genuine and unprecedented war rather than an “incident,” questioned reliance on the politically weak Wang Ching-wei, and rejected “Asia for the Asiatics” and the “new order in East Asia” as unrealistic ideals. He warned against making enemies of Europe and the United States and doubted that Japan possessed the reserves necessary for continental hegemony. The American Embassy interpreted the article as evidence of an internal Japanese policy struggle and a growing realization that implementing the aims of the Konoe statement might offer an escape from Japan's difficulties.

interest: The memorandum preserves an unusually candid Japanese critique of wartime expansion that was quickly censored and cost its author his official position. It is especially useful for studying dissent within the Japanese bureaucracy, American diplomatic interpretations of that dissent, and contemporary doubts about Wang Jingwei, pan-Asianist rhetoric, and Japan's capacity to dominate China. The routing stamps and cross-reference sheet also illustrate how information about censorship, news reporting, immigration, and diplomatic protest moved through the State Department's filing system.
